doc.title: Bobby Watson interviewed by Michael Woods, Clinton, New York, January 19, 1996

title: Dropping categories and the old circuit versus Europe
summary: Asked where jazz is going, he wants to stop categorizing, mentions electric and gospel plans, and contrasts the old American circuit with today's travel to Europe.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: I’m going to ask you one thing, and I know we’ve got to get you out of here because you’ve got to get something to eat and get dressed and maybe detox a little bit. But where is jazz going? Give me some places where it can go, or the possibilities that you see in it.

Well, I think we have to stop categorizing. Like now you know I’m doing this electric thing, and because I grew up doing it. But also I play jazz. And so you’re going to hear my things be a little bit more aggressive than what they call that soft jazz. Because we’re still up there really trying to mesh and play. But that’s not all I do. Like I mentioned earlier, I play in the church so I’d like to do a Gospel record at some point. And here’s another thing I see that really has changed the dynamics of the music. People like Lou Donaldson and Barry Harris, they’re in our generation, a lot of them just started going to Europe maybe ten years ago for the first time in their life. Meanwhile, I’m 42 right now, I’ve been to Europe maybe 70, 80 times, and all over the world. And so it used to be in the 40s and the 50s and maybe up in the early 60s when they say you do the circuit. And the circuit was basically the country. You know you did a circuit, you’d go down south, you’d go to Chicago, and that was a circuit that all the jazz guys traveled. Except Dexter and Johnny Griffin, they went to Europe, Don Byas and Coleman Hawkins, all them guys went back to Europe for a time. But basically the main circuit that everyone traveled was in America. So but you reflected off of, and then when you did get a chance to go to Europe, you didn’t really concern yourself with the locals as they would say. You’d never really hear the local musicians. They were all coming to hear you, because you had jazz. And you were there because you had something that they couldn’t find in Europe. So you tended to be a little arrogant maybe and maybe a little closed-minded about hearing some local musicians. Because I found that there are virtuosos that play their music in every country. And a virtuoso is a virtuoso. And so when you meet someone who has this level of skill, and he’s playing Greek songs or Bouzouki players what have you, clarinet players from Romania or something like this, it’s really wild stuff. And you have to open your ears to that. And they want to hook up with you because now it’s 1996 and all through the 70s, things started happening. Now in Europe they have people who are the new Coleman Hawkins, and they’re the grandfathers of European jazz and can play.
